paragraph_text: Virtually all scholars of antiquity agree that Jesus existed.
Reconstructions of the historical Jesus are based on the Pauline epistles and the gospels.
Scholars differ about the beliefs and teachings of Jesus as well as the accuracy of the biblical accounts.
The crucifixion of Jesus occurred in 1st-century Judaea, most likely in AD 30 or AD 33.
According to the canonical gospels, Jesus was arrested and tried by the Sanhedrin.
The precise date of the crucifixion has been debated.
Jesus (c. 6 to 4 BC – AD 30 or 33), also referred to as Jesus Christ, Jesus of Nazareth, and many other names and titles, was a first-century Jewish preacher and religious leader.
Most Christians believe he is the incarnation of God the Son and the awaited Messiah.
Virtually all modern scholars of antiquity agree that Jesus existed historically.
The baptism of Jesus by John the Baptist is a major event in the life of Jesus described in the gospels.
Most modern theologians view the baptism of Jesus as a historical event to which a high degree of certainty can be assigned.
The Gospel of Matthew uniquely includes a dialogue between John and Jesus before the baptism.
The Gospel of Mark is the second of the four canonical gospels and one of the three synoptic gospels.
Most scholars date Mark to around AD 66–74, shortly before or after the destruction of the Temple in AD 70.
The Gospel of Mark is anonymous and most scholars agree that it was written by an author who was not an eyewitness to the events described.
Mark's narrative can be divided into two parts: Jesus's ministry in Galilee and surrounding areas, and his final week in Jerusalem.
Mark sandwiches the cleansing of the temple between the two halves of the fig tree episode. This Markan intercalation links the two episodes structurally.
The Gospel of Matthew is the first book of the New Testament and one of the three synoptic gospels.
Matthew contains five major discourses, each concluded with the formula 'when Jesus had finished these sayings.'
The author of Matthew used the Gospel of Mark as a source, and also drew on a hypothetical sayings collection known as Q.
Matthew presents Jesus as the new Moses, delivering a new law from a mountain.
The Gospel of Luke is the third book of the New Testament and one of the synoptic gospels.
Luke's infancy narrative is written in a Septuagintal style, deliberately imitating the Greek of the Old Testament.
Luke emphasises Jesus's concern for the poor, women, and social outcasts.
The Gospel of John is the fourth of the four canonical gospels.
John employs a distinctive technique of misunderstanding: Jesus uses ambiguous language, his dialogue partner understands it literally, and Jesus clarifies the spiritual meaning.
Its theology is distinctive: it presents Jesus as the pre-existent Logos who became flesh.
The resurrection of Jesus is the Christian belief that God raised Jesus from the dead on the third day after his crucifixion.
In 1 Corinthians 15:3–8, Paul lists several resurrection appearances.
The historicity of the resurrection is debated among scholars.
N. T. Wright argues that resurrection must be understood within its first-century Jewish context.

paragraph_text: The first-century Jewish historian Josephus mentions Jesus twice in his Antiquities of the Jews.
The Testimonium Flavianum, in Book 18, describes Jesus as a wise man and mentions his crucifixion under Pilate.
Most scholars believe the passage has been interpolated by later Christian scribes.
The Roman historian Tacitus references Christ and his execution by Pontius Pilate in his Annals.
This is the earliest non-Christian reference to Jesus's death.
The Sermon on the Mount is a collection of sayings spoken by Jesus of Nazareth found in the Gospel of Matthew.
The Beatitudes (Matthew 5:3–12) open the sermon with eight blessings.
The sermon is structured around six antitheses: 'You have heard that it was said – but I say to you.'
The Sermon on the Mount has been one of the most influential texts in Christian ethics.
The Lord's Prayer is a central Christian prayer which, according to the New Testament, Jesus taught as the way to pray.
The prayer appears in Matthew 6:9–13 and Luke 11:2–4 in slightly different forms.
The doxology 'for yours is the kingdom and the power and the glory forever' is absent from the earliest Greek manuscripts.
The Parable of the Good Samaritan is a parable of Jesus recounted in the Gospel of Luke.
It tells of a traveller who is stripped, beaten, and left for dead. A priest and a Levite pass by, but a Samaritan stops to help.
The parable has been interpreted as teaching that neighbourly love transcends ethnic and religious boundaries.
The Pool of Bethesda is a pool in Jerusalem known from the Gospel of John 5:2.
Archaeological excavations in the 19th century identified a double pool structure north of the Temple Mount.
The identification of the site has been debated, though most archaeologists accept it.
Caesarea Maritima was an ancient Roman city on the Mediterranean coast of present-day Israel.
The Pilate inscription, a limestone block discovered at Caesarea Maritima in 1961, confirms Pilate's title as praefectus.
The Sea of Galilee is a freshwater lake in Israel through which the Jordan River flows.
Many of Jesus's miracles in the gospels take place on or around the Sea of Galilee.
Herod Antipas was a 1st-century ruler of Galilee and Perea, bearing the title of tetrarch.
He is mentioned in the gospels as responsible for the execution of John the Baptist and as playing a role in the trial of Jesus.
The role Herod Antipas played in Jesus's trial has been variously evaluated.
Pontius Pilate was the fifth governor of the Roman province of Judaea, serving under Emperor Tiberius from AD 26 to 36.
The sources for Pilate's life include the gospels, the works of Josephus, Philo, and Tacitus.
Scholarly assessments of Pilate have varied considerably.
The nativity of Jesus is described in the gospels of Matthew and Luke.
Matthew and Luke agree that Jesus was born in Bethlehem during the reign of Herod the Great, but differ on many details.
Most scholars regard the nativity narratives as primarily theological rather than historical.
The Last Supper is the final meal that Jesus shared with his apostles in Jerusalem before his crucifixion.
The Synoptic Gospels present it as a Passover meal, while the Gospel of John places it before the Passover.
The Last Supper provides the scriptural basis for the Eucharist.
Paul (born Saul of Tarsus; c. 5 – c. 64 or 67), commonly known as Paul the Apostle, was a Christian apostle who spread the teachings of Jesus in the first-century world.
Fourteen of the twenty-seven books in the New Testament have traditionally been attributed to Paul.
Seven of the Pauline epistles are undisputed by scholars as being authentic.
Mary Magdalene was a woman who, according to the four canonical gospels, travelled with Jesus as one of his followers and was a witness to his crucifixion and resurrection.
The Gospel of John names her as the first witness to the resurrected Jesus.
Mary Magdalene is considered by some as having been an apostle to the apostles.
The Gospel of Thomas is a non-canonical early Christian text discovered near Nag Hammadi, Egypt, in 1945.
It consists of 114 sayings attributed to Jesus.
Its relationship to the Synoptic Gospels is debated: some scholars date its core to the first century.
The Pharisees were a Jewish social movement and a school of thought in the Levant during the time of Second Temple Judaism.
Josephus describes the Pharisees as the most accurate interpreters of the laws.
The New Testament portrayal of the Pharisees as legalistic hypocrites has been re-evaluated by modern scholars.
The Sadducees were a Jewish sect active in Judea during the Second Temple period.
Josephus says they rejected the resurrection of the dead and held only the written Torah as authoritative.
The Essenes were a Jewish sect that flourished from the 2nd century BCE to the 1st century CE.
The Dead Sea Scrolls, discovered at Qumran, are widely attributed to the Essenes.
The precise relationship between the Essenes and early Christianity continues to be debated.
The Council of Jerusalem, described in Acts 15, was a meeting around 50 CE between Paul, Barnabas, and the Jerusalem church leaders.
The council decided that Gentile converts were not required to be circumcised.
The decision of the council is considered a watershed moment in the history of Christianity.
The Sanhedrin trial of Jesus refers to the trial of Jesus before the Sanhedrin, a Jewish judicial body, following his arrest in Jerusalem.
The accounts in the gospels differ in details. Mark places the trial at night, which some scholars note conflicts with Mishnaic law.
Scholars debate the historicity of the trial, with some viewing it as a theological construct.
The empty tomb is the Christian tradition that the tomb of Jesus was found empty on the third day after his crucifixion.
All four gospels report that women were the first to discover the empty tomb.
The fact that women are the primary witnesses — in a culture where their testimony was considered unreliable — has been used as an argument for the tradition's authenticity.
The Ascension of Jesus is the Christian teaching that Christ physically departed from Earth by rising to Heaven.
Luke 24:50-53 and Acts 1:9-11 describe the ascension as occurring forty days after the resurrection.
The ascension has been understood theologically as Christ's exaltation and enthronement at the right hand of God.
Jerusalem is a city in the Middle East located on a plateau in the Judaean Mountains between the Mediterranean and the Dead Sea.
The city is central to the narratives of the gospels, particularly the events of Jesus's final week.
The city holds profound significance for all three Abrahamic faiths.
Bethlehem is a city in the West Bank, Palestine, located about 10 km south of Jerusalem.
According to the gospels of Matthew and Luke, Bethlehem is the birthplace of Jesus.
Archaeological evidence for Bethlehem as a settled town in the 1st century has been questioned by some scholars.
Nazareth is the largest city in the Northern District of Israel.
In the New Testament, Nazareth is described as the childhood home of Jesus.
Archaeological excavations at Nazareth have revealed limited evidence of settlement in the early Roman period.
The Temple in Jerusalem was one of a series of structures located on the Temple Mount.
Herod the Great began a massive expansion of the Second Temple around 20 BCE.
The gospels present Jesus's action in the Temple — the 'cleansing' — as a pivotal event that precipitated his arrest.
The Olivet Discourse is the name given to Jesus's teaching on the Mount of Olives about the end times.
It appears in all three Synoptic Gospels: Mark 13, Matthew 24-25, and Luke 21.
Matthew's version expands Mark's with additional parables: the Wise and Foolish Virgins, the Talents, and the Sheep and Goats.
Interpretations of the discourse range from preterist (fulfilled in AD 70) to futurist (still to come).
The Parable of the Prodigal Son is a parable of Jesus recounted in Luke 15:11–32.
The parable tells of a father with two sons. The younger demands his inheritance, leaves, squanders it, and returns destitute.
The parable uses the structure of a double denouement: the younger son's return is the expected climax, but the older son's angry response creates a second, open-ended climax.
The Parable of the Sower is a parable of Jesus found in all three Synoptic Gospels.
The parable describes a sower who scatters seed on four types of ground: the path, rocky ground, thorns, and good soil.
The allegorical interpretation identifies the seed as the word of God and the soils as different responses to it.
The feeding of the five thousand is a miracle of Jesus reported in all four gospels.
The Synoptics place the event near Bethsaida, while John locates it on the eastern shore of the Sea of Galilee.
Scholars debate whether the event should be understood as a literal miracle or a symbolic narrative.
Codex Sinaiticus is a 4th-century manuscript of the Greek Bible, containing the earliest complete copy of the New Testament.
It was discovered by Constantin von Tischendorf at Saint Catherine's Monastery on Mount Sinai in the 19th century.
The codex is written in four columns to the page and includes both the Septuagint and the New Testament.
Codex Vaticanus is a 4th-century manuscript of the Greek Bible.
It has been housed in the Vatican Library since at least the 15th century.
Together with Codex Sinaiticus, it is one of the two most important witnesses to the text of the New Testament.
The Johannine Comma is a clause found in 1 John 5:7-8 in some later manuscripts.
It appears in no Greek manuscript before the 14th century.
Its inclusion is a well-documented example of textual corruption driven by theological pressure.
The Didache, also known as The Teaching of the Twelve Apostles, is a brief early Christian treatise.
It contains instructions on baptism, fasting, prayer, and the Eucharist.
Its precise relationship to the canonical gospels remains unclear, with scholars debating whether it represents independent tradition or distillation.
Irenaeus was a Greek bishop of Lugdunum in Gaul who lived in the 2nd century.
His work Against Heresies is a major source for understanding early Christian diversity and the development of orthodoxy.
The Nag Hammadi library is a collection of early Christian and Gnostic texts discovered in Upper Egypt in 1945.
The discovery included the Gospel of Thomas, the Gospel of Philip, and the Apocryphon of John.
The texts have been heralded as revolutionary, but their impact on New Testament studies is contested.
